--- title: "Uncertainty, Priors, and Simulation" --- Before we fit a model to data, we need to understand what it does. Model building is not a pipeline where you write the equations, press "fit," and read off the answer. It is a *dialogue* between you, the model, the data, and the decisions the model informs — a bargaining process over model complexity, the data available to constrain it, and the consequences of different intervention strategies. At each stage, you're asking a specific question and using simulation to answer it. Three kinds of uncertainty run through this entire workflow: - **Parameter uncertainty** — we don't know the "true" parameters. (The scare quotes are deliberate: epidemiological parameters are effective summaries of complex processes, not fixed properties of nature.) The transmission parameter $\beta$ might be 0.3 or 0.5, and the epidemic looks very different in each case. This uncertainty shrinks when we fit the model to data, but never disappears entirely. - **Process uncertainty** — even if we knew every parameter exactly, the epidemic is a stochastic process. Run the same model with the same parameters twice and you get different trajectories. *Demographic* stochasticity (which susceptibles happen to meet which infecteds) is the main contributor at small population sizes; on top of that, *environmental* fluctuation in the transmission rate (school schedules, weather, gatherings) pushes the dynamics around day-to-day. Both are intrinsic to the system and cannot be reduced by collecting more data — only by modeling them more faithfully. - **Observation uncertainty** — even with parameters and the underlying trajectory both fixed, what reaches us is incomplete and noisy. Surveillance catches a fraction of cases; reporting is overdispersed and delayed; serosurveys come with sample-size sampling error. The measurement layer has its own variance, and disentangling it from the process layer — telling "noisy data from a smooth epidemic" apart from "clean data from a noisy epidemic" — is one of the central jobs of inference. A single simulation trajectory ignores all three. When a decision-maker asks "should we vaccinate?" the answer depends on the *distribution* of outcomes under all three sources of uncertainty, not on one arbitrary simulated future. Carrying every kind of uncertainty forward — from model specification through simulation to the eventual policy comparison — is what separates rigorous analysis from storytelling with curves. The example files for this chapter are in [`guide/boarding-school/`](https://github.com/vsbuffalo/camdl-book/tree/main/guide/boarding-school). ## Priors — simulating from beliefs alone We don't need data to start learning about our model; in fact we *should not* bring data into the picture until we've interrogated and explored how the model interacts with our current or *prior* beliefs. The first step is to encode our prior beliefs about the parameters directly in the model file. It may seem strange to bring our beliefs explicitly into a scientific model, in light of the notion that science is "objective" and "data-driven." But the reality is that (1) every model is built on a foundation of many assumptions and beliefs, and (2) we implicitly encode "flat" or "uniform" priors for model parameters when we simply state the parameter bounds, or state parameters live on a logscale. These implicit priors can seem neutral and objective, but are actually quite strong, and can have a large influence on model inference and the conclusions we draw from it. ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## "Flat" priors are not uninformative A long tradition in Bayesian statistics has shown that uniform or "vague" priors carry more information than they appear to. [Jeffreys (1961)](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/theory-of-probability-9780198503682) first demonstrated that flat priors are not invariant under reparameterization — a uniform prior on $\beta$ is not uniform on $\log \beta$, so the choice of parameterization smuggles in information. [Jaynes (2003)](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511790423) developed this further, arguing that maximum entropy is the principled baseline precisely because uniform priors on arbitrary scales are not "uninformative." [Gelman (2006)](https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/research/published/taumain.pdf) showed that common "vague" prior specifications (like $\text{InverseGamma}(\epsilon, \epsilon)$ for variance parameters) are in fact highly informative, and [Gelman, Simpson, and Betancourt (2017)](https://doi.org/10.3390/e19100555) sharpened the point: **"informative" is a property of the pair (prior, likelihood), not of the prior alone.**[^prior-context] A distribution that looks flat in isolation can be a strong claim under one likelihood and genuinely diffuse under another — and along weakly-identified directions in the likelihood (the $R_0$–$1/\gamma$ ridge, the reporting-fraction vs. process-noise trade-off common to overdispersed fits), the prior never washes out no matter how much data you collect. Under an identified model with sufficient data, the prior's influence vanishes — the posterior concentrates around the maximum likelihood estimate ([Bernstein–von Mises theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%E2%80%93von_Mises_theorem)). So this isn't about priors dominating the analysis forever. It's about the regime where priors matter most: small data (early in an outbreak, a novel pathogen, limited surveillance) and structurally non-identified models (nearly every interesting compartmental fit). In those settings, which are exactly when decisions are most urgent, encoding domain knowledge through thoughtful priors can mean the difference between useful model-informed decisions and misleading ones. ::: Recall the parameters block from [Building an SIR Model](getting-started.qmd); these had no priors — just types and bounds. Yet these encode substantive "flat" beliefs: `beta` is a rate between 0.05 and 1.0, `gamma` is a rate between 0.01 and 0.5. These bounds rule out certain epidemics. But bounds are coarse; they say "not impossible," not "what I actually believe". Usually we have more specific beliefs about parameters values, just based on the context of the infectious disease and transmission processes. Putting this prior information into the model file makes it visible and explicit. But more importantly, it *concentrates* our beliefs into a smaller region of plausible parameter space, which greatly improves how well inference works. camdl lets you attach a prior distribution directly to the parameter declaration using the `~` operator — standard "distributed as" notation from Bayesian modeling: ```camdl parameters { beta : rate in [0.05, 1.0] ~ log_normal(mu = -1.0, sigma = 0.5) gamma : rate in [0.01, 0.5] ~ half_normal(sigma = 0.5) rho : probability in [0.1, 0.9] ~ beta(alpha = 2.0, beta = 5.0) k : positive in [1.0, 100.0] ~ half_normal(sigma = 10.0) N0 : count # no prior — fixed externally I0 : count # no prior — fixed externally } ``` Each line now reads as a complete belief statement: `beta` is a rate, plausible between 0.05 and 1.0, with a log-normal prior centered around $e^{-1} \approx 0.37$. The type, bounds, and prior are all visible at the declaration --- a reader doesn't need to look anywhere else to understand what the modeler believes about this parameter. In camdl, model priors always optional. Parameters without priors are structural constants we may treat as known or fixed (population size, initial seed count) supplied via `--params` (and held fixed during inference). Models without any priors are valid for simulation, but they are doing so either at fixed parameter values or with implicit "flat" priors, which can lead to misleading inference and predictions when data is scarce. ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Supported prior distributions | Distribution | Syntax | Notes | |-----------------|-------------------------------------|--------------------------------| | `log_normal` | `~ log_normal(mu = M, sigma = S)` | mu, sigma on the **log** scale | | `normal` | `~ normal(mu = M, sigma = S)` | mean, standard deviation | | `half_normal` | `~ half_normal(sigma = S)` | folded normal, support $[0,\infty)$ | | `beta` | `~ beta(alpha = A, beta = B)` | shape parameters | | `gamma` | `~ gamma(shape = K, rate = R)` | rate parameterization (not scale) | | `exponential` | `~ exponential(rate = R)` | rate = 1/mean | | `uniform` | `~ uniform(lower = L, upper = U)` | explicit uniform | All arguments are named (keyword), never positional. Arguments must be compile-time constants — arithmetic like `mu = log(0.3)` is fine. ::: ### Prior predictive checks Encoding priors in the model enables the first step of the model building dialogue: carrying our prior, highly-uncertain beliefs forward into simulation *without any data*. A **prior predictive check** draws parameter values from the prior, simulates the model at each draw, and examines the resulting distribution of outcomes. If the prior predictive distribution includes absurd epidemics — infecting the entire population in three days, or producing no infections at all — that's an early warning that the model is misspecified or our beliefs need revision. This check is only possible if we encode our beliefs as priors in the model; without them, there is nothing to simulate from. To see this concretely, consider our toy SIR with uniform priors — the "I have no idea" starting point: ```camdl parameters { beta : rate in [0.05, 1.0] ~ uniform(lower = 0.05, upper = 1.0) gamma : rate in [0.01, 0.5] ~ uniform(lower = 0.01, upper = 0.5) } ``` ::: {#88005a9c .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

This sounds "uninformative" but it's actually a strong statement: it implies that $R_0 = \beta / \gamma$ values of 50+ are just as plausible as $R_0 = 2$ (the log scale in the left panel makes this visible). Look at what this does to the *implied distribution of outcomes* in the right panel. The spike at zero total infections is the uniform prior telling you there is substantial probability that the epidemic doesn't happen at all — because a large fraction of the $(\beta, \gamma)$ draws produce $R_0 < 1$. If you're modeling an outbreak that observably infected 500 people, putting 20–30% of your prior mass on "no epidemic" is not uncertainty — it's incoherence. Your other beliefs (that flu is transmissible, that this is a boarding school, that an outbreak clearly occurred) are *mathematically incompatible* with the fizzle-out probability implied by uniform priors. The prior predictive makes this visible before you've touched any data. The high tail is biologically just as implausible. A uniform prior over $[0.05, 1.0] \times [0.01, 0.5]$ for $(\beta, \gamma)$ puts substantial mass on $R_0$ values above 10 — measles-grade contagiousness for what we already know is influenza. Most respiratory pathogens have $R_0$ in the range 1–5 (seasonal flu ~1.3, pandemic flu ~1.5–2, varicella ~3–5); $R_0 \geq 10$ is reserved for a small set of outliers (measles ~12–18, pertussis ~5–17). Saying "I'm uniform on $\beta$ and $\gamma$" is implicitly saying "I'm equally open to the flu I'm modeling being as contagious as measles" — not a claim of ignorance, but a claim that spans two distinct biological regimes with equal weight. Once you know the pathogen and that an outbreak is in fact occurring, both tails of the implied $R_0$ distribution carry information you don't actually believe. ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Coherence and the Dutch book The idea that beliefs must be internally consistent has deep roots. [Ramsey (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100011621) argued that a rational agent's degrees of belief must obey the probability axioms — otherwise an adversary can construct a set of bets (a "Dutch book") that guarantee the agent loses money regardless of the outcome. [De Finetti (1937)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02938457) formalized this: incoherent probabilities are operationally exploitable. What does this have to do with priors on $\beta$ and $\gamma$? The prior predictive is a *coherence audit*. Your prior over parameters *implies* a prior over outcomes — including the probability of epidemic fizzle-out. If you say "I'm uniform over ($\beta$, $\gamma$)" while simultaneously believing "an epidemic is underway," those two beliefs are incoherent: the first assigns ~25% probability to an event the second considers near-impossible. A Dutch book exists against you. The prior predictive makes this visible by computing the implied outcome distribution and letting you check it against your other knowledge before the data ever enters the picture. ::: The log-normal prior concentrates mass around more realistic values (median $\beta \approx 0.37$, median $\gamma \approx 0.14$, implying $R_0 \approx 2.7$) but is still quite broad — the 95% range of outcomes spans an order of magnitude. This is the "I think it's flu-like but I'm not very sure" prior. Better, but still too vague to be useful for a specific setting. ### From toy model to real data The prior predictive tells us something important: even our log-normal priors produce a wide range of outcomes. In practice, we'd know more — the pathogen, the population, the clinical picture. A boarding school flu outbreak in January is not a novel pathogen in a megacity. Let's ground the rest of this chapter in a real dataset: the [1978 English boarding school influenza outbreak](http://alun.math.ncsu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2017/01/influenza_78.pdf) (Anonymous, 1978, *BMJ* 1:578). This is literally the textbook SIR example — 763 boys at a boarding school in North England, 512 of whom were confined to bed with H1N1 influenza over 14 days in January 1978. The data is daily prevalence: how many boys were in bed each day. ::: {#cell-fig-boarding-school-data .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Plotting code"} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5)) ax.bar(flu_data["day"], flu_data["in_bed"], width=0.8, color="#cc3333", alpha=0.7, edgecolor="none", label="Confined to bed") ax.bar(flu_data["day"], flu_data["convalescent"], width=0.8, bottom=flu_data["in_bed"], color="#f4a460", alpha=0.5, edgecolor="none", label="Convalescent") ax.set_xlabel("Day of outbreak") ax.set_ylabel("Number of boys") ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9) ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 13.5) ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The 1978 boarding school influenza outbreak. Daily prevalence (number of boys confined to bed) over 14 days. 512 of 763 boys were eventually infected — a 67% attack rate.](experiments_files/figure-html/fig-boarding-school-data-output-1.png){#fig-boarding-school-data width=1030 height=504} ::: ::: Now we can write an SIR model with *informed* priors — beliefs that reflect what was known about influenza in 1978. By then, decades of epidemiological study had established that influenza R0 typically falls between 1.5 and 4 ([Biggerstaff et al., 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4169819/)), with an infectious period of 2–5 days. In a boarding school with communal dining and dormitories, the reporting fraction (proportion confined to bed) would be high. These are genuine prior beliefs — not arbitrary numbers, but the accumulated knowledge of the field. ```camdl parameters { beta : rate in [0.1, 5.0] ~ log_normal(mu = log(2.0), sigma = 0.5) gamma : rate in [0.1, 1.0] ~ log_normal(mu = log(0.4), sigma = 0.3) N0 : count I0 : count rho : probability in [0.5, 1.0] ~ beta(alpha = 5.0, beta = 2.0) k : positive in [1.0, 100.0] ~ half_normal(sigma = 10.0) } ``` The log-normal on `beta` centers around 2.0 (giving R0 ≈ 5 with gamma ≈ 0.4 — high for flu, but a boarding school is a high-contact setting). The log-normal on `gamma` centers around 0.4 (infectious period ≈ 2.5 days). The grey spaghetti shows the range — most epidemics peak between 250 and 350 infected, but the timing and exact shape vary. Some outbreaks (the flat lines near zero) fail to take off entirely: with only one initial infection, there's a real chance the index case recovers before transmitting. The observed peak of 298 (dashed line) falls squarely within the distribution — the model is consistent with the data at these parameters. Notice how the process uncertainty here is structured: the peak *magnitude* is fairly tight (roughly 250–380 infected, compared to the prior predictive spread of 0–500+), but the peak *timing* shifts by several days across realizations. This is a known property of stochastic SIR — the variance in peak timing scales with the time the epidemic spends near the exponential-growth phase, where small differences in early transmission compound. With 763 people, the law of large numbers constrains peak size, but timing remains noisy. The chain-binomial draws shown above capture *demographic* stochasticity: which susceptibles happen to meet which infecteds at the propensities the model specifies. They do not capture day-to-day environmental variation in the underlying transmission rate — school schedules, weather, public gatherings — which most real outbreaks exhibit. Leaving this variation unmodeled forces the observation parameters ($\rho$, $k$) to absorb extra-demographic variability they shouldn't, biasing both inference and predictions. ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Overdispersed transmission and the Euler-multinomial step [He, Ionides, and King (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2009.0151) introduced the now-standard treatment for extra-demographic variability in mechanistic epidemic models: multiply the per-step transmission rate by a gamma-distributed white-noise increment with unit mean and dispersion $\sigma^2$, so the realized hazard over an Euler step of length $\Delta t$ becomes $\beta \cdot \Gamma_{\Delta t} / \Delta t$ with $\Gamma_{\Delta t} \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\Delta t / \sigma^2,\, \sigma^2)$. The intensity parameter $\sigma$ is fit jointly with the rest of the parameters. In camdl this is written as `infection : S --> I @ overdispersed(beta * S * I / N, sigma)`. This is *still* process uncertainty — same family as chain-binomial — but adds environmental variation on top of demographic. **Is there an analytical Euler-multinomial form that absorbs the noise?** Partially. For a *single-compartment* counting process — purely additive events with a rate that depends only on time, not on the dynamic state — [Bretó and Ionides (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spa.2011.06.012) showed that integrating gamma white noise into the rate yields a clean **Negative-Binomial** transition density in closed form: the per-step event count is exactly NegBin, replacing the usual Poisson/binomial draw. For multi-compartment SIR-style flows, where the hazard $\beta S I / N$ depends on populations changing during the step, no single distribution absorbs both the gamma rate noise and the multinomial allocation. camdl handles this the standard way: draw $\Gamma_{\Delta t}$ once per Euler step, multiply it into the rate, then perform the regular Euler-multinomial draw. As $\Delta t \to 0$ this converges to the He et al. continuous-time process; in single-source outflow sub-steps (e.g. recovery alone), it reduces to the Bretó-Ionides closed-form Negative-Binomial. We use `overdispersed()` extensively in the [He et al. vignette](../vignettes/he2010.qmd), where it's load-bearing for fitting the 1948–1968 measles record. ::: Remember: we haven't fit to data yet. The parameters here ($\beta = 1.66$, $\gamma = 0.44$) are textbook values from the literature, not posterior estimates. The 1978 data (black dots) is overlaid for orientation — to check that the model *can* produce trajectories consistent with reality at these values. Actual parameter estimation comes in [Fitting to Data](fitting.qmd). ## The observation process — what the data actually looks like Everything so far has shown the *true* infected count $I(t)$ — the model's internal state. We introduced the observation model in [Building an SIR Model](getting-started.qmd): the pipeline of reporting fraction $\rho$ and negative binomial noise that stands between the true epidemic and your data. That chapter used `incidence(infection)` — accumulated new cases per observation window. The boarding school model uses `prevalence(I)` instead, because the data is a daily bed count: how many boys are confined *right now*, not how many became infected since last week. ```camdl observations { in_bed : { projected = prevalence(I) every = 1 'days likelihood = neg_binomial(mean = rho * projected, r = k) } } ``` The observation process adds a third layer of uncertainty on top of parameter and process uncertainty. In the [next chapter](scenarios.qmd), we'll put them to work: interventions that modify the model mid-simulation, scenarios that package counterfactual comparisons, parameter sweeps that test robustness, and a batch system that manages it all reproducibly. [^prior-context]: Three consequences of the (prior, likelihood) framing from [Gelman, Simpson, and Betancourt (2017)](https://doi.org/10.3390/e19100555) are worth internalizing even if you don't care about Bayesian statistics philosophically. **First, flat priors can swamp surprisingly large datasets.** Gelman, Simpson, and Betancourt re-analyze a study of $n = 3000$ survey respondents estimating $\delta$, the difference in girl-birth probability between "beautiful" and "plain" parents; the sample estimate is $0.08 \pm 0.033$. Under a uniform prior on $\delta \in [-1, 1]$, the posterior just echoes the likelihood: 99.2% probability that beautiful parents are more likely to have girls, 50% probability the effect exceeds 8 percentage points. But human sex ratios are remarkably stable near 48.5% across every demographic split ever measured (race, maternal age, season of birth, socioeconomic status), with sub-percentage-point variation outside pathological settings. A uniform prior on $[-1, 1]$ is not "uninformative" — it is a strong claim that $\delta$ could plausibly be 50 percentage points. A $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.005^2)$ weakly informative prior that merely matches what we already know about human biology collapses the posterior to a sensible 0.2 percentage points. Same data, same $n = 3000$, different conclusion. And $n = 3000$ is *not small* — but it is laughably small compared to ~4 million US births per year, which is the comparison that actually frames the prior. For ID modelers: weekly case counts from 20 years of measles surveillance feels like a lot of data, but it is not a lot of data *relative to what the likelihood needs* to pin down a 12-parameter compartmental model with overdispersion. **Second, "default" priors are already likelihood-specific.** Essentially every principled default construction in the literature is silently a function of the likelihood. Jeffreys priors are proportional to $\sqrt{\det I(\theta)}$, where $I(\theta)$ is the Fisher information of the likelihood; reference priors (Bernardo 1979) require a specified likelihood to define "maximal missing information"; regularizing priors (ridge, half-Cauchy) are designed to stabilize specific MLE pathologies. The folklore that "a principled default prior is likelihood-free" has never been true in any Bayesian method we actually use. Gelman, Simpson, and Betancourt's contribution is to drop the pretense: let priors depend on the likelihood openly, and judge them on the data-generating processes they imply when pushed through it (the prior-predictive distribution). **Third — and this is load-bearing for compartmental modeling — along non-identified directions, the prior never washes out.** Bernstein–von Mises ("priors vanish asymptotically") is a theorem about *identified* models. If two parameter combinations produce the same likelihood along a ridge — $\beta$ and $1/\gamma$ along the $R_0$ contour, reporting fraction $\rho$ and process-noise scale $\sigma$ trading off in overdispersed fits, Gaussian-process range $\kappa$ and marginal variance $\sigma^2$ along a $\sigma^2 \sqrt{\kappa}$ ridge — the posterior concentrates on a *submanifold*, not a point. The prior's projection onto that submanifold sets the answer forever: a harmless-looking prior on $\kappa$ directly determines the posterior on $\sigma$, and a flat prior on $\beta$ covertly specifies a posterior on $R_0$. More data does not rescue you. Only changes in model structure or explicit informative priors can break a structural non-identifiability. If you take one thing from the Gelman–Simpson–Betancourt paper, take this: run a parameter-identifiability check before declaring a prior "noninformative," because along ridges there is no such thing.
